endorsements.title: Promise, Mimicry, and Surveillance: Responsibly Integrating Artificial Intelligence With Socratic Inquiry in Medical Education
endorsements.quote: Before acquisition, institutions should adopt responsible-use principles such as those articulated by the Association of American Medical Colleges [ 10 ] and require the documented assessment of the specific educational gap being addressed; a data inventory specifying what is collected, how long it is retained, with whom it is shared, and when it is deleted [ 36 ]; system limitations and the thresholds at which a tool is withdrawn; a cost-benefit analysis that accounts for opportunity cost and the value of displaced educator time; and named actors accountable for ongoing audit.

commentary.bottom_line: Nine sources endorse defining measurable goals, success metrics, timelines, and expected costs and benefits before approving an AI deployment, but no supplied study tests whether doing so changes deployment outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and planning logic rather than on comparative evidence.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The nine endorsements include two frameworks, two guidance documents, and five commentaries, and only one framework uses mandatory language. Consensus of this kind supports face validity, but GRADE cannot assign certainty without studies of the practice itself.

The ambient scribe guidance ties goal setting to measuring financial value against outcomes such as burnout and productivity. No supplied study reports the staff time or cost of prespecifying metrics, or whether prespecified metrics led systems to stop or scale deployments. Feasibility at scale therefore remains an assumption in the endorsing sources.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare AI deployments approved with and without prespecified goals and success metrics, and measure whether prespecification affects decisions to continue, modify, or stop a tool, the time to those decisions, and the governance effort required.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether goals and metrics defined before deployment would capture outcomes that matter to their patients, such as equity of benefit across language or insurance groups.
